messages.subject: Distance sampling burrows
messages.body_plain:
Dear distance list,

I am helping some colleagues design a survey to monitor the abundance of
active and inactive burrows of a species of endangered rat in
Madagascar. These burrows are easily identifiable but in their forest
habitat, the detectability reduces quite rapidly from a line. As these
burrows do not move (but may change in activity) between years, we were
thinking of using a new configuration of line transects each year, so
that the same burrows were not being sampled repeatedly - and that
pooling across years would be possible for improving the detection
function if encounter rates are very low.

However, it would be beneficial to be able to monitor the fate of
indiviudal burrows over time and only permanet line transects would be
able to do this.  Additionally, permanent line transects would sample
less natural variation and produce more precise estimates for monitoring
purposes.

This may be a simple question, but are there any fundamental
problems/consequences of using permanent line transects to estimate the
abundance of stationary objects (that may change in activity between
years) for monitoring purposes?

Your thoughts and advice would be much appreciated.

Regards,

Richard Young
--

messages.subject: Re: Distance sampling burrows
messages.body_plain:
Richard, there is no problem in principle in having permanent transects
for stationary objects.  If the observer records detected burrows
independently of previous visits, then you should be able to pool data
between visits, to increase sample size for estimating the detection
function.  However, if you want to monitor individual nests, then you want
the observer to check all burrows previously detected.  A few burrows
undetected on previous visits might also be located, so that the detection
function including both burrows previously detected and newly-detected
burrows will be different (wider) than that for previous visits.  If
sample size allows, you would need to estimate the detection function
separately for each survey.  If it doesn't, you may be able to use the
covariate option in Distance, to put survey number in as a factor
covariate - or possibly as a continuous covariate (perhaps transformed),
assuming that the scale parameter shows an increasing trend with time.

Note that, at say the 2nd survey, 'new' burrows will be one of two types:
some may genuinely be new since the previous visit;  others may be burrows
present but missed in the first survey.  The latter will tend to be the
less detectable burrows - and predominantly those further from the
transect - so burrows available for detection (having eliminated those
detected in the previous survey) will not be uniformly distributed with
respect to distance from the line, so that a standard distance sampling
analysis that omits previously-detected (and monitored) burrows will be
biased.

Steve

> > I am helping some colleagues design a survey to monitor the abundance of
> > active and inactive burrows of a species of endangered rat in
> > Madagascar. These burrows are easily identifiable but in their forest
> > habitat, the detectability reduces quite rapidly from a line. As these

> > This may be a simple question, but are there any fundamental

messages.subject: g(o)
messages.body_plain:
Dear List,

We have been distance sampling badgers (Meles meles) using spotlights,
in Gloucestershire, U.K. The area is made up of mixed woodland/scrub and
open agricultural land. We found it impossible to survey for badgers in
woodland and so concentrated all our efforts on open land. From radio
tracking studies we found that badgers spend on average 48.5% of their
time on open land. From bait marking studies we know the delineation of
badger territories and therefore the area of open land and woodland for
each territory.

Our question concerns the calculation of abundance. As far as we know
this can be done either of two ways:

1. You use the 0.485 figure as a multiplier of g(0). This then
calculates what the density would be if all badgers were on the open
land at once. i.e. the abundance of the population of interest. One
obvious advantage of this method is that DISTANCE utilises the variance
associated with the radio tracking fixes, when calculating the
confidence of the density estimate.

2. You calculate the abundance of badgers on open land only, assuming
g(0)=1 (which is a fair assumption) and then use the radio tracking data
to estimate the number of badgers that weren't on the open land.
Obviously the sum of the two equals the total abundance within those
social groups.

Both these methods produce the same estimate of abundance (not
surprisingly). However, the first method seems a bit contrived (i.e.
artificially adjusting the g(0)), although it has the advantage of
including the variance associated with the radio tracking multiplier.
The second method seems more intuitive but, including the associated
variance is beyond us! Can it be done? Are both these methods equally
valid?

Any advice would be great.

Cheers,

Tim.
--

messages.subject: Re: g(o)
messages.body_plain:
Tim, Distance allows multipliers for various reasons.  There is no need to
regard it as an estimate of g(0).  The multiplier (first) method is more
appropriate, because your second method doesn't estimate the number in
woodland directly.  Rather, you still base estimation on the multiplier,
to estimate the woodland component.  Thus variance estimation is more
naturally handled through the multiplier method.  See pp57-8 and 182 of
the 2001 book.

Steve

messages.subject: WORKSHOPS: Distance sampling, Canada, March-April 2004
messages.body_plain:
DISTANCE SAMPLING WORKSHOPS
                   Ontario, Canada
                March 31st-April 7th 2004

                    1st ANNOUNCEMENT
              PRELIMINARY REGISTRATION OPEN

      http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance.workshops.canada/

The Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling (CREEM) is
presenting two linked workshops in the spring of 2004 in Ontario, Canada.   The
aim of these workshops is to train participants in the latest methods for design
and analysis of distance sampling surveys, including line and point transects.
The workshops are taught by leading researchers in the field, using industry-
standard software.

The first workshop will run at an introductory level, and will focus on
"conventional" distance sampling methods, as described in the standard reference
book Introduction to Distance Sampling.  The workshop will be a blend of theory
and practice and participants will learn how to use the program Distance.
Participants will gain a solid grounding in both survey design and methods of
analysis for distance sampling surveys.

The second workshop will cover the latest advances in distance sampling research
and software. It is intended for those already familiar with conventional
distance sampling methods.  Participants will learn the use of covariates for
modelling the detection function, double-platform methods for when detection at
the line or point is not certain, spatial modelling of density, automated survey
design and adaptive sampling.  Participants will learn the more advanced
features of Distance, and some practical sessions will use the free statistical
software R.

For both workshops, participants are encouraged to bring their own data sets,
and can expect to do some preliminary analyses with their data.

The workshops are being hosted by the Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources at
the Leslie M. Frost Natural Resources Centre, Dorset, Ontario.  With its
wonderful lakeside location, surrounded by pristine forest, the centre provides
a fantastic setting for our workshops.  Transport from Toronto (Pearson)
International Airport to the Frost Centre is part of the workshop package.

The number of participants on each workshop is limited to 35.  Places will be
filled on a first-come, first-served basis on receipt of completed registration
form and payment in full.  Judging from previous years' workshops we expect to
fill all the places, we encourage you to register early!

We are currently in the final stages of working out the registration
arrangements, and hope to open registration in a few weeks.  Meanwhile, if you
are interested in coming, we encourage you to register interest by contacting
the workshop organizer (address below).

For more information, see the workshop web pages:
http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance.workshops.canada/
which are also accessable by following links from the CREEM web site

messages.subject: Angle measurement and crabbing
messages.body_plain:
Dear List

In ship-board cetacean surveys there seem to be two main methods in =
common
use for measuring the angle or bearing of a sighting, which is required =
in
order
to calculate the distance of the sighting from the trackline. Some =
workers
use a compass to measure a bearing to the sighting, while others use an
angle board to measure the angle of the sighting relative to the heading
of the vessel.

The use of angle boards assumes that the vessel is heading along the =
axis
of the trackline. However, this is frequently not the case. Currents =
flowing
across the trackline cause the vessel to head somewhat into the =
direction
the current is coming from in order to follow a pre-determined course or
trackline, in which case the vessel is not aligned with the trackline. =
This
is known as crabbing. Lateral winds may also cause a vessel to crab. In
these circumstances, angles measured with a sightings board that is =
aligned
with the axis of the vessel will be inaccurate.

Crabbing angles vary with the strength of currents and their angle in
relation
to the trackline. Thus on a given survey day, the crabbing angle will =
change
as currents change (tidal currents are not constant but ebb and flow) =
and
with changes in trackline direction.

The situation is likely to be even worse in the case of small survey =
vessels
that may weave about from side to side in order to follow a trackline,
whereas
larger vessels using an autopilot generally settle down to a constant
crabbing
angle.

After some discussion with colleagues, two points of view have emerged =
about
this problem:

1) It does not matter because sightings are distributed randomly on =
either
side of the trackline.

2) It does matter because the potential inaccuracy can be quite large =
(of
the order of 10 degrees) and if we take care to make our distance
estimations
as accurate as possible then we should do the same for our angle =
estimates.

Angle boards are cheap to implement and simple to use. But should we be
using them for Distance sampling unless we also record the actual =
heading
of the vessel at the time angles are measured?

Mick Baines
Sea Watch Foundation
UK

messages.subject: Re: Angle measurement and crabbing
messages.body_plain:
Mark, the problem of crabbing tends to be more severe in aerial surveys,
especially helicopters.  In practice, I think this is seldom a major
problem with ship surveys, though it may be for small boats.  The real
advantage that angle boards bring is the avoidance of angles rounded to
zero degrees.  Error in the angles will lead to some bias in estimating
the detection function, but bias in estimating abundance should be very
small.  By contrast, rounding to zero degrees can generate substantial
bias in the abundance estimate.  It might be interesting to conduct a
simulation study to see just how large the error needs to be before it
really matters.

Some survey lasers automatically give angles relative to the
transect line.  Lasers tend not to be used in marine surveys, because you
can't use them to measure distances to points on water, but I've often
thought that they might still be very useful for improving accuracy of
angle estimation.  Does anyone use them for this purpose?  If so, how
effective are they?

Steve Buckland

messages.body_plain:
Dear Distance Samplers,

I am wondering if it would make sense to develop a centralised database
which includes the
Detection Curves, ESWs and even the best fitting function details for
each species,
and for each habitat and survey type.

Once, sound detection details are compiled for each species and survey
condition and type, it might present a very helpful
information to set up and plan wildlife surveys in the future.

If that idea would make sense, are there already any such approaches on
the way ?
Should this be developed, e.g. as a public web-database ?

  Thanks and best regards

       F.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Falk,

I think your idea has merit with some caveats and modifications.  First, I
don't think there is any 'standard' detection function for a given species
in a given habitat.  This is because in my experience observer differences,
for example,  can be an important factor influencing the detection function
(and observers can affect other factors such as maximum detection distance,
w).

However, if you are designing a survey and need some guidelines regarding
ESW, detections/km, variability among transects, etc. such a database could
be very helpful.  It just seems to me that it would be important for users
to understand that such a database could never be justification for use of a
specific detection function, strip width, etc.

Just my $0.02.  I would be more than happy to contribute information I have
on detecting grassland songbirds and white-tailed deer (fecal) pellet
groups, as well as dog food pellets on Penn State lawns (a class project I
do) - just a warning that these detection functions, especially those of the
dog food pellets, can differ dramatically among observers!

Duane

messages.subject: observer variability
messages.body_plain:
Dear List,

I am analyzing data from a point transect study where observer variability
is huge!  Both observers were experienced, with equally good bird
identification skills, although Observer 2 was more experienced with
distance estimation than Observer 1.  While species abundances were
comparable, the shapes of their distributions were very different.
Observer 1 tended to heap her detections in the first two intervals
resulting in left-skewed distributions as opposed to the humped
distributions of Observer 2.  It appears that Observer 1 may have been
underestimating distances.  Is there a way to adjust the distributions of
Observer 1 so that I can potentially pool both observers?  For example, if
I calculate the average proportion per distance interval across species
from Observer 1, could I use these proportions to transform those data
from Observer 1?  Is this a reasonable approach?

Thanks and Happy Thanksgiving!
Kim Ferree

U.S. Geological Survey
Fort Collins Science Center (FORT)
2150 Centre Avenue, Building C
Fort Collins, CO 80526-8118
(858) 637-6896   fax: (858) 974-3563
kimberl...@usgs.gov

messages.subject: Re: observer variability
messages.body_plain:
Kimberly,

My $0.02:

If either observer is recording incorrect measurements then any
"corrections" are a shot in the dark and not supported by your data.

If your observers actually recorded the correct distances, then differences
in their data reflect real differences in their detection processes.  It seems
reasonable that a "new" distance observer, having been repeatedly told
that g(0) must be perfect, will focus her attention near the point.  If this
is
the case, what is the problem with estimating two seperate detection
functions and make density estimates appropriately?  Any "correction" you
make will not change the fact the Pa is different for the two observers.

My best advice is to take a close look at your assumptions (g0, movement,
accurate distances, etc.).  If you believe they are met, just estimate
different detection rates for each observer (assuming the
post-stratification by observer is supported by AIC) and don't worry about
why they are different.  Don't fool with some ad hoc "correction" just so you
can pool the data.  It is unnecessary and unsupportable.

Good luck!

~Aaron Ellingson

messages.body_plain:
> > I am analyzing data from a point transect study where observer variability
> > is huge!  Both observers were experienced, with equally good bird
> > identification skills, although Observer 2 was more experienced with
> > distance estimation than Observer 1.  While species abundances were
> > comparable, the shapes of their distributions were very different.
> > Observer 1 tended to heap her detections in the first two intervals
> > resulting in left-skewed distributions as opposed to the humped

> > Observer 1 so that I can potentially pool both observers?  For example, if
> > I calculate the average proportion per distance interval across species
> > from Observer 1, could I use these proportions to transform those data
> > from Observer 1?  Is this a reasonable approach?

Kimberly, errors in distance estimation cause serious bias in point
transect sampling.  By far the best way to resolve it is through proper
observer training, and use of laser rangefinders - which now only cost
$200 in the US - substantially more elsewhere, but you can get them
shipped from the US - e.g. from www.binoculars.com <http://www.binoculars.com>.

The advanced distance sampling book is due out next year - in it, there
will be a section on estimation when there are measurement errors, but to
do anything useful, you really need to have a subset of detections whose
distances are known.  You could retrospectively have your two observers
estimate some distances to singing birds that you later determine exactly.
Of course, it is possible that the observers will behave differently now,
especially if they know that there has been a problem with their distance
estimates.

Steve Buckland
